issues.description: The UML in the problem statement specifies Ride.abbreviation as type 'char', but the solution's Ride class declares 'abbreviation' as String (and its constructor/getter use String). Meanwhile the solution's RollerCoaster constructor uses a 'char abbreviation' parameter and calls super(name, abbreviation). This mismatch (char vs String) is inconsistent across artifacts and will cause confusion and a compile error when students try to implement constructors exactly as specified by the UML.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the 'abbreviation' type consistent across all artifacts. Preferably update the Ride class to use 'char abbreviation' (change the field type, constructor parameter, and getter to char) so it matches the UML and the RollerCoaster constructor. Alternatively, if string abbreviations are intended, update the UML and all subclasses to use String consistently.

issues.description: The UML/problem statement specifies the Ride attribute 'abbreviation' as type char, but the solution implementation declares 'abbreviation' in Ride as a String while RollerCoaster constructor uses a char parameter. This mismatch of the same conceptual attribute across artifacts (problem vs. solution) creates confusion about the expected type and constructor signatures and can mislead students when implementing getters/constructors to match the UML.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the 'abbreviation' attribute consistent across artifacts. Either (A) change the UML/problem statement to declare abbreviation as String and update RollerCoaster constructor parameter to accept String, or (B) change the solution Ride class to use a char for abbreviation (private char abbreviation), update its getter to return char, and adjust all subclass constructors (e.g., RollerCoaster) to accept and pass a char. Ensure constructor parameter orders match the UML specification.
